turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I hope I'm in the right place for this... I just, well, I wanted to talk to someone because things at work have been a little—I guess "overwhelming" is the word. 

I'm a software developer, and usually I'm pretty good at juggling things, you know? But lately, I just can't seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. I've got patent notes to review, prep for these upcoming workshops, gallery deadlines I'm helping with, and team decisions that need my input. It's just a lot, which is normal, right? Everyone gets busy. But I keep finding myself just... starting whatever is loudest or most urgent, instead of what actually matters or needs to be done first. 

I don't want to sound like I'm just complaining about being busy, because I know everyone has a lot on their plate. Does that make sense, though? Is that the kind of thing you can help with?

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot organize the moving parts of their work and struggle to prioritize tasks, instead starting whatever is loudest.

turns.doctor_question: Did you struggle with focus or organization when you were growing up, such as during your school years?
turns.patient_response:
Well, um... I guess if I'm being completely honest, yeah, it might have been there a little bit back then, too. I mean, I was a good kid! I wasn't disruptive or anything like that. But, um... if you look at my old report cards from grade school, the teachers usually said I was bright, which was nice, but... they'd also write that I tended to daydream a lot. 

And, well, I did have this habit of doing my homework and then just... forgetting to turn it in. Or I'd lose the folders entirely. This was way before high school, even. I just thought I was a little scatterbrained, you know? Like, typical kid stuff. I hope that doesn't make me sound completely irresponsible... Is that the kind of thing you're asking about?

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports that teachers noted they tended to daydream a lot in grade school, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes doing their homework but forgetting to turn it in, which aligns with failing to follow through and finish schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly mentions a habit of losing their homework folders entirely.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or like you have trouble sitting still for long periods?
turns.patient_response:
Um, well... I wouldn't say I'm bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I mean, I'm an adult, I can behave myself in a meeting. 

But, I guess... if I'm really thinking about it, on those really long design calls we have? I do start to feel this... this kind of pressure building up in my body to just get up. I try really hard to look focused, you know, for the team. But I end up pacing around my office a lot while I'm listening. Or, um, I'll just keep shifting from chair to chair. 

I usually just tell myself I'm trying to get comfortable, but... yeah, I guess I do have a hard time just staying put for the whole thing. I mean, a lot of people get a little antsy on long calls, right? I hope that doesn't make me sound too unprofessional. Is that the sort of thing you're looking for?

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes squirming or fidgeting by stating they 'keep shifting from chair to chair'.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to leaving their seat when expected to stay put, noting they 'end up pacing around my office a lot while I'm listening' to long calls.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms feeling physically restless, describing a 'pressure building up in my body to just get up' and feeling 'antsy'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself interrupting people or finishing their sentences before they have a chance to complete their thought?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... no, I don't think I do that. I really try my best to be a good listener. I'd hate to ever come across as rude or, you know, like I'm talking over someone or rushing them. 

I usually just stay quiet and let people finish what they're saying. I mean, if I'm being completely honest, I might get a little distracted in my own head sometimes while they're talking, but I definitely make sure to wait my turn to speak. I really value being respectful in conversations. 

I hope that's helpful? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient admits to getting distracted by their own thoughts while others are talking.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient denies finishing people's sentences and states they let others finish what they are saying.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states they make sure to wait their turn to speak.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient denies interrupting or talking over others.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you're constantly 'on the go,' as if you're driven by an internal motor that's hard to turn off?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no... no, I don't think I feel that way. I definitely wouldn't say I'm constantly on the go or, you know, driven by a motor or anything. 

I mean, I work in software development, so I actually spend a lot of my day just sitting at my desk, looking at code. I'm pretty low-key, honestly. I definitely like to have some downtime in the evenings to just relax and unwind. I'm not one of those people who always has to be out doing something or running around. 

I try to keep things pretty balanced, you know? I hope that's an okay answer. I just don't really relate to that feeling of always having to be moving. Does that make sense?

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling constantly on the go or driven by a motor, stating they are pretty low-key and don't relate to always having to be moving.
